title: Where the data sleeps
tagline: Storage keeps being reinvented by the same pendulum: give up structure for scale, then spend a decade putting the structure back.

events.title: IBM 350 RAMAC
events.summary: Five megabytes on fifty spinning platters — and the first time a computer could reach a record without winding through the ones before it.

media.alt: Disk platter motif for the RAMAC

keyPoints: Random access, as opposed to tape's strictly sequential reading.
About one ton, five megabytes, and rented rather than sold.
Made interactive queries against live business records conceivable.
Every index, B-tree, and access-path decision since assumes this machine's descendant.
events.impact: Random access is the hardware fact that made databases a category. Sequential storage gives you batch reports; addressable storage gives you a query.

events.title: IMS
events.summary: A hierarchical database built to track the bill of materials for a Saturn V, and a demonstration of what pointer-walking costs you.
keyPoints: Data is a tree; a query is a program that navigates it.
Extremely fast for the access path it was designed around, and only that one.
Changing the physical layout meant changing every program that read it.
Still in production in banking and insurance, decades on.
events.impact: The thing Codd was arguing against. IMS worked, which is exactly why the cost of hard-coded access paths needed a paper to make it visible.

events.title: The relational model
events.summary: Ask for data by what it is, not by where somebody put it — the idea the rest of this rail keeps rediscovering.

media.alt: Table motif for the relational model

keyPoints: A relation is a set: order and physical layout carry no meaning.
Physical data independence — storage can change without rewriting applications.
The query optimiser exists because the query no longer names an access path.
Normalisation targets update anomalies, not tidiness.
events.impact: Declarative querying became the default interface to data, and the optimiser became the most valuable component in any data platform.

events.title: Oracle V2
events.summary: The first commercial SQL database, shipped by a company betting that a research idea could be sold before IBM finished shipping it.

media.alt: Lock and transaction motif for Oracle

keyPoints: There was no V1; the version number was a sales decision.
ACID transactions made concurrent access a solved problem for application authors.
Locking and isolation levels are where the theory meets a contended production system.
SQL became a standard in 1986, which turned a product into a skill.
events.impact: Made the relational model commercially inevitable and made SQL a portable skill — the reason an engineer can move between vendors without relearning how to ask a question.

events.title: The data warehouse
events.summary: Notices that the questions a business asks about its history are a different workload from the transactions that made it.

media.alt: Racks motif for the data warehouse

keyPoints: Analytical reads and transactional writes want opposite physical layouts.
Inmon argued top-down from an enterprise model; Kimball bottom-up from dimensional marts.
Slowly changing dimensions are the durable idea: history is a modelling problem, not a backup.
ETL becomes a named discipline, and a permanent source of operational cost.
events.impact: Separating analytics from operations is now assumed. Every modern lakehouse, warehouse, and read replica is a version of this split.

events.title: Hadoop
events.summary: Google's two papers, rebuilt in the open, so that anyone with a room full of cheap disks could process more data than would fit on one machine.
keyPoints: Move the computation to the data, because moving petabytes is the expensive part.
Commodity hardware plus replication beats reliable hardware on cost.
Schema-on-read: store first, decide what it means later.
That last one is also how the data swamp got created.
events.impact: Made storing everything cheap enough to be the default, which set up the next fifteen years of work putting structure and governance back on top of it.

events.title: Hive
events.summary: SQL over MapReduce — the declarative layer comes back within four years.

events.title: Spark
events.summary: Keeps working sets in memory between stages, and makes iterative jobs practical.

events.title: Presto
events.summary: Interactive SQL straight against the lake, with no ingestion step in between.

events.title: The cluster dissolves
events.summary: Object storage plus elastic compute makes owning a permanent cluster look expensive.

events.title: Dynamo
events.summary: Decides that for a shopping cart, always accepting a write matters more than every replica agreeing on what it says.
keyPoints: Consistent hashing, vector clocks, and eventual consistency in one production system.
Availability is chosen over consistency, deliberately and with the business reason stated.
Conflict resolution is pushed up to the application, which knows what a merge means.
Started the NoSQL decade — and much of the industry read only the headline.
events.impact: Made the CAP trade-off a concrete engineering decision rather than a theorem, and produced a generation of stores that were right for some workloads and adopted for all of them.

resources.label: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store

events.title: Parquet
events.summary: Stores a table down its columns instead of across its rows, which is what analytical queries were asking for all along.
keyPoints: Read only the columns the query names; skip the rest of the bytes entirely.
Values of one type sit together, so compression and encoding get dramatically better.
Row-group statistics let a reader skip whole blocks without decoding them.
An open format, so the file outlives the engine that wrote it.
events.impact: The default physical format for analytical data. Separating the file format from the query engine is what made engines interchangeable.

events.title: Separating storage and compute
events.summary: Puts the data in object storage and rents the query engine by the second, so the two stop having to be sized together.
keyPoints: Storage scales with the data; compute scales with the questions being asked.
Independent warehouses over one dataset end the contention between teams.
Elasticity turns capacity planning into a billing decision.
The architecture, not the SQL dialect, was the product.
events.impact: Reset the expectations for every data platform. Warehouses, lakehouses, and streaming engines are now all judged on whether they can scale the two halves apart.

resources.label: Choosing a data platform by workload

events.title: Open table formats
events.byline: Iceberg at Netflix, Delta Lake at Databricks, Hudi at Uber
events.summary: Adds a transaction log over the files, so a directory of Parquet finally behaves like a table again.

media.alt: Pipeline motif for open table formats

keyPoints: A metadata layer gives atomic commits, snapshot isolation, and time travel.
Schema evolution stops being a rewrite of the whole dataset.
Several engines can read and write the same table without a shared server.
The pendulum completes its swing: the lake gets its structure back.
events.impact: Closes the loop this rail opened. Fifty years after Codd, the industry's answer to "where should the data live" is again a table with a schema and a transaction — just spread over object storage.
